name: CrateDB
license: Apache 2.0 (every feature since 4.5, March 2021); CrateDB Cloud is a paid managed service
summary: A distributed SQL database built on Lucene: every column is indexed and stored column by column, so one cluster answers aggregations, full-text, geo and vector queries over fresh machine data.
intro: CrateDB is a shared-nothing cluster written in Java. Each table is split into shards spread over the nodes, and each shard is a Lucene index made of immutable segments. Every column is indexed by default: text with a plain (whole-value) inverted index, or a full-text one if you give it an analyzer; numbers with BKD trees for range filters. Alongside the indexes it keeps doc values, Lucene’s column-by-column storage, which is on by default and serves sorting, grouping and aggregations without reading whole rows. A write is routed by its primary key (or `CLUSTERED BY` column) to a primary shard, logged in that shard’s translog, then applied on the replicas in parallel before the client gets an answer. New rows become visible to queries when the shard refreshes, once a second by default while the table is busy, or on `REFRESH`; lookups by primary key read the translog and see a write at once.

Clients speak SQL over the PostgreSQL wire protocol (port 5432) or an HTTP endpoint (port 4200, which also serves the Admin UI). Rows behave like JSON documents: `OBJECT` columns can add sub-columns on insert and are queried as `payload['firmware']`. `MATCH` runs BM25-ranked full-text search, geo types support shape queries, and `FLOAT_VECTOR` columns (up to 2,048 dimensions) answer `KNN_MATCH` nearest-neighbour searches through Lucene’s HNSW index. Tables can be partitioned by a generated column such as `date_trunc('month', ts)`; each partition gets its own shards, filters on the partition column skip whole partitions, and a `DELETE` that covers a partition drops it. There are no transactions: each row write is atomic, `BEGIN` and `COMMIT` are accepted and ignored, and concurrent updates are handled with row version numbers.

All of CrateDB is Apache 2.0. Crate.io offers it as CrateDB OSS, CrateDB Enterprise (self-hosted with support) and CrateDB Cloud, a managed service on AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and STACKIT. Since October 2026 the company and CrateDB are owned by Crate.io AG, a holding company in Vaduz, Liechtenstein. Version 6.5.0 came out on 13 October 2026.
strengths: Indexes everything by default and stores columns too, so ad-hoc filters and aggregations over billions of rows work without designing indexes first
Search, analytics and documents in one SQL dialect: full-text with BM25 scores, geo shapes, vector kNN and nested `OBJECT` columns sit next to `GROUP BY` and joins
Scales out on its own: shards are created (by default `max(4, data nodes × 2)`), replicated and rebalanced automatically, and time-partitioned tables make old data cheap to drop
PostgreSQL wire protocol, so pgjdbc and tools such as Grafana’s PostgreSQL data source connect without a special driver
limits: No transactions: atomicity is per row, `BEGIN`/`COMMIT` are silently ignored, and the PostgreSQL interface reports `read uncommitted`
Queries see new rows only after a refresh, up to a second later by default; only primary-key lookups are read-after-write

Postgres-compatible on the wire, not in the dialect: no `JSON` type (use `OBJECT`), no `TIME` without time zone, no `COPY` sub-protocol, and full-text functions differ, so many Postgres tools only partly work
Upgrades can mean rebuilding: tables created before 5.x must be recreated to run on 6.x, and a new shard count only applies to partitions created afterwards

goodFor.why: Every column is indexed and kept as doc values, so ad-hoc filters and aggregations work on rows a second after they arrive.
Tables partitioned by a generated time column skip whole partitions in queries and drop old ones with a single `DELETE`.

specs.data-model: Relational tables with nested `OBJECT` columns that can add fields on insert
specs.wire-protocol: PostgreSQL wire protocol and an HTTP endpoint
specs.secondary-indexes: Every column indexed by default: inverted indexes, BKD trees, HNSW for vectors
specs.transactions: None; each row write is atomic, and `BEGIN`/`COMMIT` are ignored
specs.consistency: Queries see new rows after a refresh (1 s by default); primary-key reads see them at once
specs.storage-format: Lucene segments per shard, with doc values as a column store
specs.scaling: Shared-nothing; shards are created, replicated and rebalanced automatically
specs.replication: Primary shard with replicas, written in parallel before the client is answered
specs.deployment: Self-hosted (OSS or Enterprise) or CrateDB Cloud on AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and STACKIT

note        TEXT INDEX USING FULLTEXT WITH (analyzer = 'english'),

-- Aggregation over doc values, the column store

-- Full-text search on the same table, ranked by BM25

story: CrateDB began in Dornbirn, Austria, where Christian Lutz, Bernd Dorn and Jodok Batlogg founded Crate in 2013 to build an open-source clustered database for fast text search and analytics; the first release came in April 2013. The founders had about ten years of history with Elasticsearch, including running some of Europe’s largest deployments. They started with their own Apache-licensed Elasticsearch plugins, such as `inout` and `timefacets`, which were merged into CrateDB, and built SQL on top of Elasticsearch’s clustering and Lucene’s indexes. Crate won TechCrunch Disrupt Europe in London in October 2014.

CrateDB 1.0 shipped in December 2016, after more than a million downloads, the same year the company moved its headquarters to San Francisco while development stayed in Austria. CrateDB 2.0 in May 2017 brought the first Enterprise Edition. With 4.0 in 2019 the team stopped tracking Elasticsearch directly and copied the code into its own repository, and the company adopted an open-core model that founder Christian Lutz later called a mistake. When Elastic moved Elasticsearch to the SSPL and Elastic License in January 2021, Crate.io said it would no longer use it as an upstream, and CrateDB 4.5 in March 2021 put every feature, including user management and privileges, under Apache 2.0; revenue was to come from support and CrateDB Cloud.

CrateDB 5.0 followed in July 2022 and 6.0 in July 2025. In October 2026 a newly formed holding company, Crate.io AG in Vaduz, Liechtenstein, took over the US company’s assets, including the Austrian subsidiary that holds the code, and Crate.io added STACKIT, a European cloud, as a CrateDB Cloud option.

choices.choice: SQL on Elasticsearch’s clustering and Lucene’s indexes
choices.why: The founders already ran large Elasticsearch clusters, and its Apache licence let them build on it freely; Bernd Dorn wrote that they would not have chosen it under the GPL. Lucene supplied the indexes underneath.

choices.choice: Copy the Elasticsearch code in, then drop the upstream
choices.why: From 4.0 the team wanted control over the modules it used, so it copied the code and only backported fixes. Elastic’s 2021 licence change ended any reason to follow Elastic’s releases.
Existing drivers and tools then work unchanged: pgjdbc connects, and Grafana reaches CrateDB through its ordinary PostgreSQL data source.

choices.choice: One Apache 2.0 codebase instead of open core
choices.why: Christian Lutz wrote that over 85% of paying customers wanted a managed service anyway, that features such as authentication mattered to every user, and that a single codebase was simpler to develop and to partner on.
